item.title: From Nest to Deathbed, Jackie the Eagle Entranced California and Beyond
item.description:
A bald eagle whose loves and losses riveted millions via a livestream of her lifelong nest died in a California animal hospital on Monday.

The eagle, known as Jackie, gained worldwide fame during the Covid-19 pandemic, as a bored public became enraptured by her life in the rugged San Bernardino Mountains. Viewers tuned in to watch her soaring, nesting and squawking over a landscape that was suddenly far less filled with the affairs of human beings.

Jackie raised eaglets with two mates in the same nest where she was born in 2012, atop a 120-foot-tall Jeffrey pine in Big Bear Valley, a lakeside recreation area in Southern California.

Then last month, she fought off an apparent attack on the ground by other eagles, defending herself by rolling on her back and slashing at them with her talons.

She wasn’t injured, but she was unable to fly. Rescued by park workers, she was taken to the Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation center hundreds of miles away in Ojai, Calif.

Jackie underwent extensive medical treatment there as fans tracked her plight on social media. The center’s staff found several underlying medical conditions, including kidney inflammation and severe anemia, that Jackie was unable to overcome.

Chris Eksteen, the center’s executive director, posted that Jackie had most likely been sick for some time.

Bill Bowerman, a professor of wildlife ecology and environmental toxicology at the University of Maryland, said it was likely that the young eagles seen attacking Jackie in a video were probably “hungry and thought that Jackie was sitting on the shoreline with a fish.”

They were likely unaware of her weakened condition, he said.

Jenny Voisard, a spokeswoman for Friends of Big Bear Valley, a nonprofit conservation group that operates the webcam trained on Jackie’s nest, agreed with that assessment. “They were just being eagles, and trying to take her fish and potentially territory,” she wrote in an email.

The raptor center announced Jackie’s death on Monday. “We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the center said in a Facebook post.

“It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her,” the center added.

Jackie hatched in the spring of 2012 and rose to fame in 2015, when a camera was installed on her parents’ nest, which she eventually took over along with her mate, Mr. B. In 2018, a new male, later named Shadow, arrived and pushed Mr. B out.

Fans watching the livestream weighed in as Jackie and Shadow attempted to start a family. Viewers mourned after some of Jackie’s eggs were determined non-viable and scavenged by ravens and celebrated the births of healthier offspring. Recent sightings of a younger female perching near Shadow created a flurry of tabloid-style speculation, but experts said it was unlikely that either eagle was looking for a new mate.

Last month, after a decades-long effort by conservationists to protect Jackie’s habitat from development, Friends of Big Bear Valley announced that it had received $10.5 million in donations, allowing the group to create a sanctuary for the eagles and other wildlife.

At the raptor center, which is about two hours northwest of Los Angeles, concerns and then condolences poured in via social media and the postal box on Monday.

“Every day I check the mail, there have been probably 50 letters for Jackie in there,” said Ethan Van Dusen, office manager for the neighboring Ojai Valley Land Conservancy, which shares the mailbox, shortly before news of the eagle’s death was posted.

“People are sending donations,” he said. “Someone sent salmon from Alaska. Someone sent Fiji water because they wanted her to drink water that was pure.”

item.title: Trump Wants to Move On From the Middle East. It’s Not Letting Him.
item.description:
President Trump may want to let go of the Middle East. But it won’t let go of him.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump said his new strategy was to be “low-keying it” in Iran, a suggestion that he wants to pressure the country into making a favorable deal without taking major military action. But a stark reminder of the limits of U.S. power in the region came from Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared Sunday he was “ruling out” Mr. Trump’s peace plan for Gaza.

The two Middle East conflicts have underscored Mr. Trump’s eagerness to declare success and his inability to impose his will on them, despite the enormous military firepower that he has been able to deploy.

Mr. Trump is “clearly trying to find a pathway as the midterms approach to downgrade all of this,” said Brian Katulis, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. Instead, Mr. Katulis went on, “reality is slapping him in the face.”

Mr. Trump faces depleted weapons stockpiles, an Iranian regime determined to impose pain on the United States, an Israeli prime minister battling for re-election and American voters reeling from high prices induced by the Iran war. The November midterms keep ticking closer, steadily raising the political costs of the turmoil to Mr. Trump and Republicans.

Mr. Trump laid out his low-key approach to Iran in a brief interview with the news website Axios on Sunday. Rather than make new military threats, he said that “we are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.” He added: “It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game.”

“Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Monday, acknowledging Iran’s ability to keep harassing commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. “But they’re broke.”

In describing the Iranian regime as suffering from economic pressure, Mr. Trump evoked his own predicament. The average price of a gallon of gasoline remained above $4 this week, more than $1 above the price when the United States and Israel began bombing Iran on Feb. 28. Polls show even Republicans growing disenchanted with the Iran war and Mr. Trump’s political movement has fractured over his decision to launch military action.

“I don’t think the president has very good options,” said Suzanne Maloney, an Iran specialist and vice president at the Brookings Institution in Washington. “The pressure points for the Iranians are, while real, more endurable and bearable than those that are impacting the U.S. economy and the strategic calculus of the administration.”

A White House official said in a statement on Monday that Mr. Trump’s “bold actions” on the battlefield in Iran and in diplomacy over Gaza “will strengthen American security for years to come.”

“The failed Obama and Biden policies were defined by appeasement,” said Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman. “The successful Trump policy is defined by American strength.”

In Gaza, Mr. Trump trumpeted a “historic breakthrough” on July 30, a multiphase deal under which the militant group Hamas would eventually disarm and Israel withdraw from the Palestinian enclave. Writing on his Truth Social website, in all capitals, he hailed an “amazing development” that “everybody said could never be achieved.”

But in the days after Mr. Trump announced the plan, Gaza saw an increase in deadly Israeli bombings. On Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu, who earlier this year went into the Iran war alongside Mr. Trump, emphatically rejected Mr. Trump’s plan: “I want to be clear here — Israel is ruling out the 15-point document.”

The Gaza episode was, to some analysts, another reminder of diminished American influence in the Middle East in the wake of the Iran war, which has dragged into its sixth month with none of Mr. Trump’s expansive goals appearing close to being accomplished. Many Israelis have seen Mr. Trump’s pursuit of a peace deal with Iran as a betrayal, giving Mr. Netanyahu a political incentive to be seen as standing up to Mr. Trump as he seeks re-election in October.

In both Iran and Israel, Mr. Katulis said, Mr. Trump has “misread the regional power dynamics.” Mr. Katulis also pointed to the new defense pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as a sign of countries looking to hedge their bets amid uncertainty over the future of American power in the Middle East.

In Iran, for all of Mr. Trump’s efforts at finding a way out, a renewed flare-up of violence could come at any moment. The U.S. military has kept up its naval blockade of shipping to Iranian ports and said Saturday it had redirected 53 commercial vessels in recent weeks, along with disabling two ships and boarding two others. Mr. Trump’s enormous buildup of U.S. military force in the region, including two aircraft carrier groups, has remained in place.

“These tools are not low-key,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, an expert on Iran at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that is hawkish on Iran, referring to the U.S. sanctions and blockade. “Iran is likely not going to take them lying down.”

The United Arab Emirates on Saturday said an Iranian attack had targeted a tanker belonging to one of its state-owned oil companies as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz, the major artery for oil shipments out of the Persian Gulf. The Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia in Yemen, have threatened to block Saudi oil shipments through the Red Sea.

A senior Iranian official said on Saturday that Iran would reopen the strait only if the United States met a sweeping list of demands, including lifting sanctions and the blockade. The official, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, also demanded war reparations, prompting Mr. Trump to post on Truth Social on Monday that “I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran.”

Iran’s compensation, he said, would need to cover people killed and wounded in Iran’s “many conflicts” as well as Iranian protesters killed by the regime. He said he had instructed officials to seek that compensation in “any, and all, future negotiations.”

Iran and the United States are not known to be negotiating directly, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that Iran and neighboring Oman were holding talks with U.S. input. Online, some of the loudest supporters of Mr. Trump’s initial decision to bomb Iran continued on Monday to push for new attacks.

“For those here and elsewhere living in a fantasyland, there will need to be further military action,” the Fox News host Mark Levin wrote on X. “Economic pressure alone won’t cut it.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

]]>

item.title: Homeland Security Intensifies Pursuit of Noncitizens on Voter Rolls
item.description:
The Trump administration is making an intense push to identify and deport noncitizens who registered to vote, even if they did so inadvertently or never cast ballots — an unusually aggressive approach that is helping it promote baseless claims that voter fraud is rampant.

State audits and studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and there have been no instances in which their votes are known to have swayed an election. It is against federal law for noncitizens to register to vote or actually vote, and doing so can carry steep penalties, including jail time and deportation.

In the past, the Department of Homeland Security has not aggressively tried to deport the relatively small number of noncitizens who unlawfully registered to vote, especially if they mistakenly signed up, according to immigration policy experts. But the Trump administration is taking a harder line in hopes of increasing deportations while also building a case that illegal voting has been underestimated.

Homeland security agents are reopening voter fraud cases that had been closed and investigating voter registration efforts in major cities. Customs officers have detained immigrants suspected of being on the voter rolls at border checkpoints, according to immigration attorneys. And green card holders applying for citizenship have been placed in deportation proceedings for registering to vote.

The department’s efforts are part of the Trump administration’s extraordinary attempt to leverage federal agencies to promote the president’s long-running false claims about a broken election system rife with fraud. Those claims have been used by Mr. Trump to justify his push for federal legislation that would require that people show proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote and severely restrict voting by mail.

The changes are upending the lives of some green card holders who have lived in the United States for years and maintain that they did not vote or even intend to register.

Abdullah Emre Basar first learned that he was on the voter rolls in Washington State when he applied for citizenship and an immigration officer at his interview last year informed him that he was registered, according to a court filing last month.

Mr. Basar later learned that he was registered in 2014 after visiting the local motor vehicle agency to update his address, said Devin Theriot-Orr, his attorney. The government denied him citizenship and placed him in removal proceedings in April, according to the filing.

Mr. Basar maintains that he never voted or asked to register. Ryan Dosch, a manager at the Spokane County elections office, said in an email that a voter registration record under Mr. Basar’s name was canceled and had no history of a ballot cast.

“It brings a lot of worry and uncertainty,” Mr. Basar said in a statement. “It is putting stress on my marriage, as my wife is a citizen and the unknown is very stressful.”

The administration’s actions have involved a close partnership between the Homeland Security Department and the Justice Department, which has sought to investigate and criminally charge noncitizens with illegal voting. Prosecutors have been instructed to file more charges against those individuals, and the Justice Department has sued dozens of states to obtain voter rolls. The department has also seized on revelations by New Jersey officials that a software glitch led to about 6,600 noncitizens being registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. Roughly 400 of them later cast ballots.

Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the Justice Department’s civil rights division, has said officials are ready to arrest or deport those who improperly voted in New Jersey. Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, indicated she would resist the Trump administration’s demands to turn over the names of the registrants, who she said ended up on the voter rolls “through no fault of their own.”

Homeland security officials are devoting significant resources to the effort, ordering agents who typically focus on transnational crimes like human trafficking and drug enforcement to hunt for voter fraud, a major shift for an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement known as Homeland Security Investigations.

In June, agents with the unit accompanied F.B.I. agents during a raid of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a group that conducts voter registration drives, and actively questioned staff members.

“Conducting voter fraud investigations is a real departure for H.S.I., and is not within the normal scope of their very important criminal investigative work,” said Deborah Fleischaker, a senior ICE official during the Biden administration.

In a statement, a homeland security spokesperson said that ICE was rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it could be found.

The Trump administration has also prodded states to upload tens of millions of voter records through SAVE, a federal immigration verification tool run by the Homeland Security Department that the administration revamped to look for noncitizens on the voter rolls.

But there have been problems with the SAVE tool itself. In October, Jane Nelson, the Texas secretary of state at the time, announced that her office had identified 2,724 potential noncitizens who were registered to vote in Texas. But local election officials who looked into the findings at the county level found that many identified by SAVE were actually citizens. An independent investigation in Travis County, Texas, home to Austin, found that 25 percent of the noncitizen matches were citizens, according to court records.

Homeland security officials have continued to push evidence-free claims of widespread election fraud. Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said last month that the administration uncovered more than 250,000 cases of noncitizens registered to vote in four states, but provided no evidence to support the finding or details about how officials arrived at that number.

Letters from the Homeland Security Department to some states indicated that the number was probably overestimated, with caveats and based on initial reviews. Some state officials, including in Nevada, have cast doubt on the methods the department used to calculate the estimate.

The intense focus on deporting noncitizens on the voter rolls marks a shift for the Homeland Security Department. Several immigration attorneys said they had clients who were still approved for citizenship under previous administrations if they explained that they mistakenly registered and had no other issues with their cases.

Michael Valverde, who was a senior official at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for more than two decades, said that immigration officers used to have some ability to take into account factors like intent, age and mental capacity in considering whether registering to vote or voting rendered them removable.

“Now officers have very limited discretion, and I am hearing that denials and removal proceedings based on voting are happening more frequently,” Mr. Valverde said.

Attorneys said many of their clients who registered did so inadvertently while obtaining or renewing driver’s licenses, pointing to voter laws that have made it easier for people to register to vote at motor vehicle agencies. Some immigrants lack English fluency and do not realize they are signing registration forms, lawyers said.

Altagracia White, a 61-year-old resident of Woodbury, N.J., who is married to a U.S. citizen, said the federal government was seeking to deport her. Ms. White said she first learned that she was registered to vote after she applied for citizenship and an immigration officer informed her. Ms. White later obtained documents from the state showing that she signed a voter registration application while renewing her driver’s license more than a decade ago.

“I never thought they were telling me to sign to vote or anything like that,” Ms. White said. “At that time, I didn’t even know how to say yes in English.”

The federal government has initiated her deportation to the Dominican Republic, citing her voter registration and claiming she voted in 2020. County records show that Ms. White voted once via mail-in ballot that year. Ms. White denied that she sent the ballot or ever voted.

George Fishman, a deputy general counsel at the Homeland Security Department during the first Trump administration, praised the agency’s efforts to pursue noncitizen voting. Although he said there was a “certain level of unfairness” when it came to noncitizens who inadvertently registered to vote, he thought it was Congress’s responsibility to pass reforms that would prevent them from getting onto voter rolls.

“I think the most vigorous enforcement should be against those who knew they were voting illegally, but the law needs to be enforced,” said Mr. Fishman, a senior legal fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, an organization that supports lower immigration rates.

Coral Murphy Marcos contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Trump Stokes Islamophobia by Calling Democratic Candidates ‘Jihadists’
item.description:
President Trump on Monday described Democratic candidates in the midterm elections as “jihadists,” adding to Islamophobic statements recently made by Republican elected officials.

Mr. Trump also delivered another tirade against people of Somali descent, saying: “They’re not smart, they have no aptitude, they have nothing going, and they’re telling us how to run our country.”Asked about the candidates representing the Democratic Party in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that “we have jihadists being elected all over the place. We have this — whether it’s communism, jihadism.”

White House officials did not respond to requests for comment about Mr. Trump’s statements on Monday, and about how the comments could alienate Muslims in the United States.

Throughout his rise in politics, Mr. Trump has vilified Muslims and people of Arab descent, stoking anger among his backers and building support for immigration restrictions, including banning Muslims from the United States. But in the past few months, anti-Muslim rhetoric has become increasingly normalized in the ranks of the G.O.P., particularly after the election victories of prominent Muslim politicians, including Zohran Mamdani in the New York City mayoral race and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary last week.

Mr. Trump has declined to condemn such rhetoric, and, as was the case on Monday, has leaned into it.

While the president did not name a specific candidate, he targeted Mr. El-Sayed hours later when he posted an image depicting the Democratic candidate standing in front of a crowd that included two women wearing head scarves. “They are coming for your home and your belongings,” a caption read along the image.

And his rant came two days after he posted on social media an image of himself with the first lady, Melania Trump, next to an image of Dr. El-Sayed and his wife. The text above the image read: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.”

Asked on Sunday about the social media post, Dr. El-Sayed hit back at Mr. Trump, telling CNN that the image of the Trumps displayed “people who don’t like each other but joint in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you.” The image of himself and his wife, he added, showed “two people who genuinely love each other.”

Mr. Trump’s post also included Dr. El-Sayed’s full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. After Dr. El-Sayed’s primary victory last week, the National Republican Senatorial Committee debuted a campaign ad showing his full name, accusing him of being “the most radical Senate candidate in America.” The ad tried to link Dr. El-Sayed to a designated terrorist group.

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina and the chair of the senatorial committee, denied in an interview with CNN that the G.O.P. was trying to use the ad to spotlight Dr. El-Sayed’s Muslim faith.

“We’re going to focus and bring attention to the fact that not only is he sympathetic for Hamas, not only does he run around with Hasan Piker — someone who said that Americans deserved 9/11 — he should be held account for exactly where he stands and what he’s for,” Mr. Scott said, referring to the progressive podcaster who campaigned with Dr. El-Sayed and has since described his comments about Sept. 11 as “inappropriate.”

A number of other Republicans have ramped up their anti-Muslim language since Dr. El-Sayed’s primary win. Senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama wrote on social media that “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST,” calling him a “TERRORIST.” Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina said on social media that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”

Most senior Republican officials have remained silent, except Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician, who condemned the language used by some of his peers.

“The Muslims that I typically work with are doctors working in a remote area of Louisiana who otherwise would not have a physician unless Dr. Mohammed actually agreed to move there and be their doctor,” Mr. Cassidy said, adding that “you have to take every community in its totality.”

“I condemn those statements,” he said on CBS. “And everyone should be treated as an individual.”

Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the national deputy director for CAIR, a Muslim civil rights and advocacy group, criticized Mr. Trump’s statement about Muslim candidates.

“All Americans have the right to engage in public service, regardless of their race or faith,” he said. “By describing American Muslim public servants as threats to our nation, President Trump is putting a target on the back of Muslim elected officials across our nation.”

Mr. Trump’s comments about people of Somali descent were his latest targeting the community. Last December, he said that Somali immigrants were “garbage,” and that he did not want them in the United States. Last month, the president shared a video on social media of Somali kindergartners in Minnesota, along with the comment, “Every girl is in a hijab … in kindergarten.”

“They come from, let’s say, as an example, Somalia,” Mr. Trump said on Monday. “They come in and then they tell us how to, how our Constitution, how our Declaration of Independence, how it works. It doesn’t work that way.”

Asked during an interview with The New York Times earlier this year if he was concerned about painting members of the Somali community the same way, Mr. Trump said, “I don’t care.”

item.title: Trump Said to Have Secretly Used Military Jet to Leave Turkey Amid Threats
item.description:
Top administration officials engaged in an elaborate deception to spirit President Trump out of Turkey during the NATO summit there last month, transporting him in a catering container to a military jet because of a threat against him and Air Force One from Iran, two senior U.S. officials said on Monday.

Mr. Trump and other officials had said publicly that he would be leaving Turkey on July 8 aboard one of the older versions of Air Force One rather than a luxury 747-8 donated by Qatar that he had flown in on. Mr. Trump told reporters at the time that he was making the switch for “old time’s sake.”

Mr. Trump boarded the older plane from the left-side door in view of cameras, and news organizations, including The New York Times, reported that he had traveled on it to Britain, where he switched back to the newer plane. The Times reported at the time that the decision was driven in part by concern about the security of the new plane donated by Qatar, which had not been equipped with all of the defensive capabilities of older versions.

But instead of flying out aboard that older, powder blue, modified 747, Mr. Trump was whisked off that plane via a catering container that had been lifted to the opposite side of the plane from where the journalists traveling with him boarded, one of the U.S. officials said. The president was then taken to a third plane, which he flew in secret to Britain, the official with knowledge of the matter said.

Reporters on the older plane were not told that Mr. Trump had not flown with them from Turkey to an air base in Britain, making them unwitting participants in the ruse and leaving them, along with some White House staff members, to serve as unknowing decoys.

After Mr. Trump arrived in Britain, he was secretly moved back to the older version of Air Force One. He then disembarked in view of reporters and walked across the tarmac to the plane donated by Qatar, which he flew to Washington.

The elaborate plan appears to have been developed in a matter of hours after officials determined that a threat against Mr. Trump from Iran was credible. It came after years of threats against Mr. Trump from Iran and amid the war he launched against that country. And it was an unusual instance of the public being deceived about a president’s whereabouts.

Officials have not previously acknowledged that Mr. Trump was not where they claimed he was. The furtive operation was reported earlier by the Washington Post, which identified the plane that carried the president to Britain from Turkey as a C-32A, a military variant of a Boeing 757.

It is rare for presidents to travel without the reporters who comprise the press pool designated to be with them, or in their vicinity, without some general awareness of the commander in chief’s whereabouts.

President George W. Bush kept a slimmed-down press pool with him as he flew first to a military base and then back to Washington in the chaotic hours after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. And presidents — including Mr. Trump — have traveled to war zones with reporters alongside them.

Donald Mihalek, a former Secret Service agent who worked in the protective details for Mr. Bush and President Barack Obama, said the Secret Service has used decoy motorcades and flights in the past to move presidents secretly.

“Anytime the president is in a theater where there’s potential combat danger, the Secret Service has employed protective counter measures including the use of a decoy,” Mr. Mihalek said.

He added that the agency has long prioritized the security of the president over transparency with the public.

“The agency is not the agency of public affairs,” he said. “The agency is the agency of the Secret Service. Their number one job is to keep the president safe.”

In this case, the threat led the White House to purposely mislead reporters assigned to cover Mr. Trump, leaving journalists to report that he was traveling on board a plane that was being used as a decoy.

After The Times reported last month on the security shortcomings of the Qatari-donated jet amid the concerns about the threat from Iran, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, seemed to hint that subterfuge might have been involved in Mr. Trump’s departure from Turkey.

“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal — including distraction and misdirection — to address those threats,” he said at the time.

The threat from Iran was not specific to the Qatari-donated jet, people familiar with the sequence of events said. Instead, Mr. Trump was being targeted on whatever airplane he was traveling on, as The Times has previously reported.

Mr. Trump was briefed on the threat while in Turkey, and a plan was soon put in place, with a small group of top government officials involved, including Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the official with knowledge of the deception plan said.

The Defense Department and a spokesman for General Caine referred all questions to the White House on Monday. The White House reissued Mr. Cheung’s statement from the week of the NATO summit, only without the clause mentioning “distraction and misdirection.” The U.S. officials with knowledge of the deception plan spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security issues.

When Mr. Trump arrived at the airport to leave Turkey, a camera that had been positioned beforehand captured him getting on the old Air Force One, and journalists traveling with him, rushing to board the plane through lower steps in the back, had only a glimpse of him. A pool report noted as the plane took off, “We have been advised to keep our window shades in the press cabin closed.”

The older Air Force One landed at 10:16 p.m. at the Mildenhall military base in England, a pool report said, with Mr. Trump stepping off it 40 minutes later. Before that, unbeknown to reporters, Mr. Trump was brought by vehicle from the third plane that he had arrived on to the older Air Force One, boarded it through a different entrance and strode down the step from the upper left-side door as he would typically do, according to the U.S. official.

He walked from there to the Qatari jet, as the small group of reporters who had traveled aboard the older jet watched. The president and the press pool then boarded the new plane to fly back to Washington.

When asked by reporters during that flight back to the United States about why they had flown on the old Air Force One to England, Mr. Trump claimed he had wanted the troops stationed at the U.K. base to see the new plane. When pressed on why the window blinds had been directed to be shut on the flight from Turkey, Mr. Trump said that he knew of no specific threat, but described himself as under constant siege from Iran.

“I’m number one on their list, before you,” he told the reporters. “But if I go, you go. Right?

Mr. Trump and a number of his advisers have faced threats from Iran for years, especially after Mr. Trump, during his first term, ordered the killing of a powerful Iranian commander, Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani.

Mr. Trump’s advisers during the 2024 campaign privately told allies that they were given intelligence that Iran still hoped to harm Mr. Trump. That led to the occasional use of decoy planes during the campaign. His staff at times put the candidate aboard a secret jet, without alerting the media, while his staff flew his private plane. The Biden administration increased security for Mr. Trump that summer after new intelligence about plots to kill Mr. Trump; a short time later, he faced an unrelated assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania at an outdoor rally. There was a second unrelated attempt in September 2024.

The collective threats, which ranged from a prosecuted murder-for-hire plot by an Iranian proxy to the hacking of Trump campaign officials’ email and social media accounts, created a siege climate for the candidate and his aides. It led to fear, insularity and, at times, paranoia, that shaped how officials interacted with the Biden administration, which was responsible for allocating Secret Service resources, as well as with the media, and with other government officials.

After the Times reported about the security concerns in Turkey, and the fact that the Qatari jet lacked the same defensive capabilities as the older presidential aircraft, Mr. Trump was enraged by the leaks. The Justice Department issued subpoenas for grand jury testimony to the reporters who had been on the bylines of the stories, as well as some of their family members. Those subpoenas were withdrawn after a federal judge admonished federal prosecutors for the process involved.

Mr. Trump has continued to rage about information coming from his government that contradicts what he is telling the public, particularly about the war in Iran that he began on Feb. 28, according to multiple officials.

Katie Rogers, Erica L. Green and Doug Mills contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Californians Criticize Federal Efforts to Control the State’s Coast
item.description:
For more than half a century, the California Coastal Commission has been entrusted with protecting the state’s 840-mile shoreline, which is integral to the state’s identity and economy.

However, the Trump administration views the agency as a blockade to development and has sought to curb its power.

On Monday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a public hearing in Santa Monica, Calif., the first step in the administration’s review of the powers of the commission and other bodies that oversee California’s coast.

Keelin Kuipers, acting director at NOAA’s Office for Coastal Management, who led the hearing, said that during the evaluation, the agency would consider the extent to which California had implemented and enforced programs, addressed coastal management and adhered to the terms of grants or loans from the federal government.

The hearing was attended by hundreds of people, including members of the coastal commission, business owners, scientists and coastal activists.

Many people at the hearing warned that limiting the powers of the commission would set California back decades, with potentially devastating consequences.

Amid a federal push for more offshore oil production and a broader rollback of environmental protections, several also said they viewed the review as a pretext for the Trump administration to bypass California’s stricter regulations.

“This isn’t about performance — this is about power,” said Maureen Ellenberger, a resident of Santa Barbara, a seaside enclave that suffered a devastating oil spill in 2015 from a pipeline that the Trump administration reopened this year over the state’s objections.

Under the Coastal Zone Management Act, a 1972 federal law, states can develop programs to manage the seashore. In California, the commission is the principal agency charged with that responsibility.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has criticized California for impeding federal priorities, particularly spaceport development and offshore oil production. Mr. Lutnick said in a letter this year that the state had a “long record of obstructing technological innovation, economic development, and related Federal efforts in the name of environmental extremism.”

Kate Huckelbridge, the coastal commission’s executive director, said at Monday’s hearing that a separate federal review of the agency last year had found “strong performance” but that the review had never been finalized. “Still, we welcome a fair and transparent evaluation,” she said. “Our record speaks for itself.”

The timing and possible outcomes of the review remain unclear, but the coastal commission said that its program could be decertified or that it could lose the 10 percent of its budget that comes from federal grants. Its partner agencies could also lose federal funds.

In an interview after the hearing, Ms. Huckelbridge said that while the Trump administration was pursuing California now, dozens of states had similar coastal management programs that could be threatened. “It really sets a terrible precedent for other states all around the country,” she said.

California’s shoreline is one of its most valuable resources, drawing millions of tourists and locals and contributing tens of billions of dollars to the economy annually. Voters created the commission in the 1970s to maximize public access to the coastline.

But the deep blue state’s laws and agencies that limit coastal development have been a persistent target of conservatives, including President Trump.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly and publicly berated the commission, which once tried to stop him from erecting a 70-foot flag on a golf course he owns near Los Angeles. The agency has also clashed with Elon Musk, a Trump ally, over the frequency of SpaceX rocket launches.

This year, California sued the Trump administration over its restarting of the shuttered oil pipeline off the coast of Santa Barbara by invoking the Defense Production Act, a 1950s-era law that has typically been used in national emergencies.

Environmental activists and many state officials see the administration’s actions as a sign that it wants to override California’s approach to coastal protection.

Joel Reynolds, a lawyer and strategist for the Natural Resources Defense Council, said at a news conference before the hearing that the federal government’s “denial of climate change, deregulation of environmental safeguards, disdain for the rule of law and disregard for science and even for basic facts” fall outside the bounds of normal policy disagreement.

The Trump administration has prioritized new oil and gas drilling, while cutting support for solar and wind power and electric vehicles.

The state’s history with offshore oil drilling, including a huge spill off the coast in 1969 that helped spur passage of national environmental legislation, makes many residents wary of the administration’s efforts.

Lindsey Horvath, a county supervisor whose district includes some of America’s most scenic coastal communities, including Santa Monica, Malibu and Venice, said that Los Angeles County, the nation’s largest urban oil field, was banning new drilling and phasing out existing wells.

“We know what’s best for Los Angeles County, for California, and for our nation, and we will never stop fighting to protect it,” Ms. Horvath said.

item.title: Jake Whisenant, Who Raced Up Yosemite’s El Capitan at Record Speed, Dies in a Fall
item.description:
Jake Whisenant, an elite rock climber who set a record for one of the fastest ascents of El Capitan in Yosemite National Park in 2024, died in a climbing accident in California’s Sierra Nevada last week, the authorities said on Monday.

The Tulare County Sheriff’s Office said that Mr. Whisenant, 30, died in Sequoia National Park after suffering traumatic injuries in a fall while climbing on Aug. 2. He was found dead by rangers after a two-day search, the National Park Service said in a statement.

Bailee Moore, a friend of Mr. Whisenant’s, confirmed his death in a phone interview.

Mr. Whisenant became known in the climbing community for his ambitious speed climbs. In October 2024, he and Brant Hysell recorded the fastest climb of Lurking Fear, a 2,000-foot route on El Capitan, the granite monolith in Yosemite National Park. The route typically takes four days to complete, but Mr. Whisenant and Mr. Hysell reached the top in 2 hours 55 minutes and 32 seconds.

“We both tapped into a flow state, fully committed to our plan, and most importantly had an absolute blast on our favorite rock,” Mr. Whisenant wrote on social media at the time.

Climbing on El Capitan has drawn a wider audience in recent years, particularly after the 2018 documentary “Free Solo” chronicled a ropeless ascent of the formation by Alex Honnold, a prominent climber. That same year, Mr. Honnold and Tommy Caldwell became the first team to complete the so-called Nose route, which runs up the middle of the rock face, in under two hours.

The previous record for Lurking Fear had been set at 3 hours 4 minutes in 2003 by Yuji Hirayama and Nick Fowler. Mr. Whisenant and Mr. Hysell carried lighter supplies as they tried to break the record, after scaling the same route in a little over four hours two days earlier, Mr. Whisenant told Gripped, a climbing magazine.

The pair set another record in June 2025 for climbing The Prow, a route on Yosemite’s 1,100-foot Washington Column, in 2 hours 52 minutes, according to a group that tracks Yosemite climbing records.

In May, Mr. Whisenant and Noah Fox climbed El Capitan twice in one day on the Nose, a rare feat on a physically demanding route that normally takes days to climb.

Mr. Whisenant, who was born and raised in Scottsdale, Ariz., was living in Mammoth Lakes, Calif., a town near Yosemite National Park, with his fiancée, Emma London, at the time of his death, Ms. Moore said.

item.title: New Evidence Shows Agents Using Slurs, Bolstering Profiling Claims
item.description:
Since immigration agents began carrying out a string of big, aggressive sweeps last year, civil rights groups have argued that the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has been defined by brazen racial profiling.

Now, body-camera footage, text messages and other documents emerging from lawsuits around the country reveal how race and ethnicity have figured in the dragnets that unfolded in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis and other U.S. cities.

In several instances documented in court filings, federal agents referred to targets as “tonks” — a derogatory term typically used to refer to Mexican immigrants and intended to echo the sound of agents’ flashlights striking their heads. Migrants suspected of being undocumented were described as “wet,” shorthand for the slur wetback. And an agent who led an operation in Southern California later described the appearance of individuals he considered suspicious: “older Hispanic males.”

Yet even as evidence of racial profiling has come to light, what seemed like settled law — that law enforcement officers could not question or detain someone solely based on their race or ethnicity — has turned out to be far more of an open question when it comes to immigration enforcement.

Last year, the Supreme Court took a step toward upending a half-century of jurisprudence when Justice Brett Kavanaugh gave a provisional blessing to such racial profiling by agents seeking out undocumented immigrants. The government has maintained that their operations are constitutional.

The lawsuit that led to the court’s temporary decision and other similar suits are still working their way through lower courts, and it could be months before they are resolved and years before the Supreme Court has a chance to say more.

In the meantime, civil rights lawyers are continuing to amass what they hope will be a valuable trove of evidence that racial profiling by immigration agents is prevalent — and that it is unconstitutional in the manner that it is being carried out today.

In 1975, the Supreme Court cleared the way for some degree of racial profiling in immigration enforcement when the justices allowed race and ethnicity to be one of the factors — but not the only one — used by agents deciding when to stop a car on suspicion that the occupants include undocumented immigrants.

Jennifer M. Chacón, a Stanford law professor who studies immigration law, said the current wave of cases — and the Supreme Court’s recent order — engages with the question of whether the 1975 decision, in U.S. v. Brignoni-Ponce, still holds.

“Is this still good law, and even if it is, when does agency behavior cross the line of what is permitted?” Professor Chacón said.

The latest batch of depositions, videos and surveillance records in Los Angeles, first reported by CalMatters and The Los Angeles Times, show that immigration agents and officers were focused on finding “day laborers.” But civil rights groups argue that their vague and varying explanations for whom they were looking for often defaulted to anyone who looked Latino, had darker skin or spoke English with an accent. That reliance on perceived race and ethnicity, they argued, also ended up unlawfully sweeping up U.S. citizens.

In one sworn declaration, a driver in a traffic stop in San Bernardino, Calif., said an officer told him he had been pulled over “because he looked like a ‘paisa,’” a slang term for a Mexican compatriot or newly arrived immigrant.

In another declaration, Angel Santiago Tafolla, a U.S. citizen in Anaheim, Calif., said that agents chased him — a dark-skinned Latino man — while ignoring his light-skinned co-workers at the Orange County carwash. One agent discharged a Taser, arcing electricity in front of Mr. Tafolla, whose clothes were wet from his work. He was handcuffed and loaded into a van, according to the document.

“I kept saying ‘I’m American,’ but they just kept telling me I was Latino and my documents were false and to stop talking,” he said.

Such encounters were not limited to California. In more than a dozen lawsuits filed in courts across the country — including in Alabama, Illinois, Oregon and Minnesota — civil rights lawyers argue that residents, predominantly Black and Latino, were wrongly targeted based on their appearance, specifically their skin color, perceived ethnicity, accents and work attire.

At least 65 U.S. citizens were described as having been stopped, questioned or detained, and because all of them were eventually released, they were able to provide lawyers with detailed accounts of their encounters with immigration agents. Some said officers refused to accept their passports or valid drivers’ licenses as proof of citizenship. Several were threatened with Tasers, tackled and handcuffed. A few were held for hours before being released, according to court filings.

Many of the filings depict federal agents as working under crushing pressure to meet a new national quota, which for a time was as high as 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The increase — a near threefold increase in May 2025 from the prior base line — forced officers to shift from individualized investigations to street sweeps intended to round up as many people as possible. Roving teams of officers in unmarked S.U.V.s repeatedly converged on Latino neighborhoods and businesses, including carwashes, Home Depot parking lots, construction sites and shopping corridors, the court records state.

“For the individuals that they’re stopping, they don’t have any information about them other than the demographic profile that they appear Latino and working class,” said Mayra Joachín, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union working on the Los Angeles case.

Government lawyers maintain in court filings that immigration operations have been highly targeted, and that isolated examples of derogatory or inflammatory language are not evidence of an agencywide policy or intent. They also argue that agents have broad powers to question people they believe are not citizens of the United States, particularly when they are only briefly stopping someone to investigate their legal status and not necessarily to conduct an arrest.

In an emailed statement, Katherine Currie, a homeland security spokeswoman, did not respond to questions about agents using slurs. She called allegations that federal officers were engaged in racial profiling “disgusting, reckless, and categorically false.”

“What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — not their skin color, race or ethnicity,’” Ms. Currie said.

For more than 50 years, courts have taken the Fourth and Fifth Amendments, along with the 1975 Supreme Court ruling to mean that immigration agents cannot stop or detain people without a specific, factual basis for believing they are in the country illegally and that race or ethnicity cannot be the sole factor in targeting someone.

Federal law has granted immigration officers far more latitude at immigration checkpoints and within a 100-mile radius of any of the nation’s borders. But civil rights groups argue Border Patrol agents have been exercising those powers deep in the interior of the country.

Now, as the cases move through the courts, the rulings will determine whether federal agents are exclusively relying on race and ethnicity to stop, question and detain people for immigration violations — and whether the limits banning such tactics will remain in place.

Kevin R. Johnson, an expert in immigration law and a professor at University of California, Davis, said that most recent Supreme Court order and accompanying opinion from Justice Kavanaugh had emboldened federal officers to rely on racial profiling nationwide.

But he cautioned that the emergency order was not the last word. The newest footage — taken from inside patrol vehicles in Chicago and Los Angeles — could raise fresh concerns for the justices when the underlying lawsuit almost certainly returns to the Supreme Court for full consideration, he said.

“The racial slurs are troubling and coupled with the recent string of Latinos killed in car stops and detention centers, they are likely to get the justices thinking about what is going on here in ways that they haven’t,” said Mr. Johnson, a former dean of the law school at U.C. Davis.

In videos from Chicago, agents point out people on the street as “tonks.” The slur has been used since at least the 1990s by immigration officers along the nation’s Southern border.

The epithet is echoed in the latest batch of video evidence filed in the Los Angeles case. More than a dozen body-camera and bystander videos capture agents bypassing people who appeared white, moving instead to question and detain men who appeared Latino nearby.

In one video, taken Aug. 6, 2025, a group of heavily armed, masked agents in camouflage cluster in the back of a moving truck, peering out. A backpack is visible on the floor.

“Whose backpack is that? Tonk?” one agent asks. “Tonk backpack?”

In most of the other footage, agents appear to be casual as they drive, joking and speculating about how successful raids had been.

“They filled three vans,” one agent says to another as they drive through a Los Angeles neighborhood on June 19, 2025. Later, one of those agents recounts seeing a man sitting in a minivan whom he did not end up approaching. “I’m pretty sure he was wet,” he says.

]]>

item.title: Will the Left Keep Winning in the Midwest? What to Watch in Tuesday’s Primaries.
item.description:
The Democratic Party’s ascendant left flank, looking to build on its success in Michigan last week, faces fresh tests in two primaries in the Midwest on Tuesday.

A democratic socialist appears to be clearly ahead in the governor’s race in Wisconsin, and a progressive is facing off against a moderate in an expensive Senate race in Minnesota. Wisconsin, like Michigan, is a closely watched national battleground.

On the Republican side, President Trump’s choice to succeed Senator Lindsey Graham in South Carolina — Mr. Graham’s younger sister, Darline Graham — is running in a special primary election against four more experienced rivals. Despite Mr. Trump’s endorsement, a runoff is likely in the crowded race.

Mr. Graham’s death last month rocked South Carolina politics, leading to Tuesday’s special primary election to succeed him. His sister, Ms. Graham, accepted Gov. Henry McMaster’s appointment to complete her brother’s term, but then she surprised South Carolina Republicans by deciding to run for a full six years in the Senate — with Mr. Trump’s support.

Special elections, especially those run on a compressed calendar, can be unpredictable. Four other Republicans also decided to run, increasing the likelihood that a runoff will be necessary on Aug. 25.

Ms. Graham, as the interim senator running with Mr. Trump’s endorsement, is the presumed front-runner. But she was untested and largely unknown before her appointment. And she has spent much of the last couple of weeks in Washington, D.C., casting votes in the Senate rather than meeting with voters and doing local media interviews to become better known.

An advocate for people with disabilities, she is running for office for the first time against more experienced campaigners: Representative Ralph Norman, who came in third in the Republican primary for governor in June; Representative Russell Fry; former Gov. Mark Sanford; and Mark Lynch, a businessman who lost the Senate primary in June to Mr. Graham.

The front-runner for the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin is State Representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist. While her victory on Tuesday is assured by most accounts, where she does well — or less well — could reveal clues as to whether the socialist brand can work in a general election in a purple state. More moderate Democrats worry that candidates with “socialist” by their names would struggle to win in America’s heartland, risking the party’s chance at a governorship in November.

Far-left candidates including Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan last week, have tended to do best among white and college-educated voters. More moderate Democrats fear that trend might suggest that other slices of the electorate that the party has counted on, including Black voters, could stay home in November. How well Ms. Hong does in Milwaukee, for instance, will be closely watched as election results come in.

Ms. Hong, 37, a chef who has been a state legislator for five years, has talked about abolishing the police, raising taxes on high earners and eliminating Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She has backed away from some of her previous statements in the closing days of the campaign.

She faces David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, who has been endorsed by Gov. Tony Evers, the outgoing Democratic incumbent. The Democratic nominee is likely to face Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican from western Wisconsin who is close to Mr. Trump.

The race between Representative Angie Craig, a moderate who represents a purple suburban district in the Twin Cities area, and Peggy Flanagan, the state’s progressive lieutenant governor, has drawn inevitable parallels to the Michigan Senate primary last week. In that contest, Dr. El-Sayed, the progressive, narrowly defeated Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate.

The Minnesota race ranks among the most expensive in state history. Though Republicans have not won a statewide race since 2006, the party’s front-runner this year, Michele Tafoya, has strong name recognition as a veteran sports broadcast journalist.

Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat, is retiring and has endorsed Ms. Flanagan, who also has the support of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Ms. Flanagan has promised to fight for a single payer health care system known as Medicare for All and to vote for suspending military aid to Israel. But unlike Dr. El-Sayed in Michigan, she is a sitting office holder who has had to face questions about a fraud scandal in state-run safety net programs under Gov. Tim Walz.

Ms. Craig, much like Ms. Stevens, has received support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Left-wing candidates have harnessed enthusiasm and turned it into actual votes by engaging in superior messaging and organization on the ground. Their better-funded rivals in the party establishment have tended to struggle this year in executing those same basics.

Should the far left continue notching victories on Tuesday, the gap in how the party factions handle the nuts and bolts of collecting cellphone numbers and email addresses, recruiting volunteers and later turning out voters to the polls could become even more apparent. So too could the reality that the left’s messages are resonating more deeply with the Democratic base.

Critics of the party’s progressive wing counter that field organizing is not enough to win a general election, when a candidate’s message must appeal to a wide swath of mainstream voters.

]]>

item.title: Democrats Plan New Push to Defeat Max Miller in Ohio After Abuse Accusations
item.description:
The Democrats’ congressional campaign arm has added Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker running for Congress in Ohio, to a list of candidates who party leaders believe can flip their districts. It is the latest sign of political fallout from the abuse allegations against his Republican opponent, Representative Max Miller.

Mr. Poindexter’s addition to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s highly competitive “Red to Blue” program is likely to attract a significant influx of campaign cash from donors. He is running for Ohio’s Seventh Congressional District, which was considered solidly Republican until Mr. Miller was accused of physically abusing family members, including holding a gun to his ex-wife’s head and fracturing his young daughter’s collarbone.

On Monday, as the deadline for Mr. Miller to withdraw passed, the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan group that analyzes elections, moved the race from “Likely Republican” to “Tossup.”

“Brian Poindexter is exactly the kind of leader Ohio families deserve in Congress — a union ironworker who has spent his life working alongside the people he’s running to represent,” Representative Suzan DelBene, a Democrat of Washington and chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in a statement. “Max Miller has never lived that reality.”

Mr. Miller, a scion of one of Ohio’s wealthiest families, defiantly stayed in the race despite pressure from within his own party to step aside. Republican officials from Washington to Ohio have warned that the scandal could cost them a seat as the party tries to keep control of the House. Mr. Miller has forcefully denied the allegations against him and accused his ex-wife, who is the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, another Republican of Ohio, of fabricating stories to sabotage his political career.

Some Republicans have stood by Mr. Miller and dismissed the allegations as a nasty custody dispute.

Mr. Poindexter has spent the last eight months campaigning without support from Democratic Party leadership, who had viewed the race as a long shot. Until last week, his campaign had not been able to raise enough money to air ads on television this fall. A longtime friend of Mr. Poindexter’s from his time on the local City Council serves as his campaign manager, communications director and head of finance all in one.

Mr. Miller has said he will lend $1 million of his own funds to his campaign. He plans to spend more than $760,000 on ads starting in September, according to AdImpact.

The Democrats have elevated 32 candidates to their “Red to Blue” program. On Tuesday, the campaign committee also added Christina Hines in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District to the list.

Candidates in the “Red to Blue” program receive strategic guidance, training and staff support, depending on timing and what each campaign needs. In this year’s primary cycle, the committee’s picks have produced mixed results, as the party base has repeatedly rejected the establishment in favor of candidates who are running as political outsiders.

The November elections will further test the program’s savvy at picking winners in key races.

Mr. Poindexter, a self-described “regular guy” running a campaign aimed at speaking to the working class, is the type of candidate Democrats believe can win over voters who have flocked to President Trump in recent years.

“This campaign started in my campaign manager’s garage last January, when we built the wooden lectern for our launch with our own hands,” Mr. Poindexter said in a statement. “This Red to Blue designation is proof of what we can build together.”

The Democrat is hoping to represent a Cleveland-area district that, with slightly different boundaries, went for Mr. Trump by double digits last year. But a version of the district also opted for Sherrod Brown when he ran for Senate in 2018, giving Democrats hope of a comeback in November.

item.title: Wildfire Forces Evacuations in Big Sur, Along California’s Famed Central Coast
item.description:
A wildfire along Central California’s celebrated Big Sur coast spread rapidly on Monday, prompting evacuation orders in Monterey County, including at several well-known destinations.

The Timber fire started Sunday in the Los Padres National Forest near Loma Vista, a Monterey County community about 100 miles south of San Jose. By Monday evening, the blaze had burned more than 1,700 acres and was 5 percent contained.

Evacuation order

Evacuation warning

Source: Cal Fire William B. Davis and Joey K. Lee/The New York Times

The authorities issued evacuation orders for several areas that covered landmarks including Nepenthe, a cliffside restaurant, and the Henry Miller Memorial Library, an arts center named for the writer who spent nearly two decades in Big Sur.

Rugged terrain and heavy vegetation were making it difficult for firefighters to reach the flames, officials said. Conditions were expected to remain dry enough overnight to keep the fire active at higher elevations, according to the U.S. Forest Service.

“I know there is a lot of uncertainty right now,” Sheriff Tina M. Nieto said Monday evening. “I want everyone to remain calm, but I also want you to pay attention and be prepared.”

Authorities were still investigating the cause of the fire.

A section of Highway 1, the famed costal route that runs through Big Sur, reopened Monday after being closed Sunday from Point Sur Lighthouse to Vista Point.

Light winds, haze and widespread smoke were forecast for the Big Sur region on Tuesday. The region’s proximity to the coast makes it vulnerable to gusts.

Judson Jones contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Says It Revoked More Than 175,000 Visas Under Trump
item.description:
The State Department said on Monday that under the Trump administration it had revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign citizens whom it accused of committing crimes and endangering the safety of Americans.

Most of the visas were rescinded over a variety of criminal accusations, including drug offenses, driving under the influence, assault, sexual assault, child abuse and fraud, the department said in a news release. Some visas were revoked over what the State Department called attempts to abuse the immigration system. The statement did not specify the exact time period when the visas had been revoked.

The New York Times could not independently confirm the identities, nationalities or visa statuses of people who were affected. The State Department’s release did not include names or details of where people were when their visas were revoked.

Visas were also rescinded from people who had celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk, the State Department said, citing comments it said were made by visa holders, including that he had “died too late” and that “when fascists die, Democrats don’t complain.”

The Trump administration has been cracking down on visa holders, particularly those it has accused of celebrating violence against Mr. Kirk, a right-wing activist who was fatally shot in September, and other Americans.

The State Department said it was “committed to using every tool available to protect our communities” from people who it said abused visas.

Several people were set to be deported on foreign policy grounds, including Iranians connected to the country’s government, a Cuban with connections to an operation run by the country’s communist leadership and a Kuwaiti who called Americans his enemy, the State Department said.

item.title: Trump Picks Project 2025 Co-Author for Role That Would Oversee Any Reflecting Pool Review
item.description:
President Trump has chosen Dennis Kirk, a co-author of the right-wing road map known as Project 2025, as inspector general for the Interior Department, a role that would oversee any review of the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The White House announced the nomination of Mr. Kirk, a former adviser to Tulsi Gabbard when she served as director of national intelligence, and a staff member at the conservative Heritage Foundation, last week. His nomination is subject to Senate approval.

The Trump administration’s efforts to rush through repairs to the pool, a national landmark, ended in disaster earlier this year. A hastily installed blue lining began to peel up and new water-purification systems failed to prevent a huge bloom of algae that turned the pool green.

Officials have said the work will be redone to fix the problems. Mr. Trump has blamed vandals, without citing evidence. The Justice Department cited a botched installation and moved to dismiss vandalism charges against several defendants.

Under Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, the department approved no-bid contracts for vendors, citing tight deadlines, in an effort to bypass scrutiny of the renovations, according to a New York Times investigation.

Last week, Democrats called on the office of the department’s inspector general to investigate the process. The office does not discuss its investigations, and it is not known whether there is one underway.

Democrats criticized Mr. Kirk’s nomination to a watchdog position that would oversee any review. Representative Jared Huffman of California said in a statement last week that it was an attempt by the White House to put his supporters in offices intended to investigate the administration.

Mark Greenblatt, who held the nonpartisan inspector general position before being ousted as part of a mass firing last year, said the nomination raised serious concerns and called on the Senate to reject the nomination. “Inspectors general must be able to investigate the administration that appointed them without fear or favor,” he said in a statement.

The White House defended the nomination in a statement on Tuesday. “Dennis Kirk has a long career within government demonstrating a loyalty to the rule of law,” it said. “We look forward to Mr. Kirk being confirmed as the next inspector general at Interior.”

Mr. Kirk recently worked as an adviser to Ms. Gabbard, who resigned in May as national intelligence director. As an associate director at the Heritage Foundation, he also co-wrote part of Project 2025, a large-scale policy playbook that detailed extreme executive branch overhauls.
